items.title: 13.2.1 Derivative as the rate of change of velocity

blocks.text:
The rate of change is a fundamental concept in describing the motion of an object moving in a straight line. In physics, this is typically analysed using position, velocity and acceleration, which are all related through derivatives (rates of change).
The position versus time graph provides a simple interpretation of the average velocity over a given time interval.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
A word about the heading. The section shows that velocity is the rate of change of position: velocity is the derivative of the position function \(s(t)\). (The rate of change of velocity itself is acceleration, which you will meet in physics and later in calculus.)
Position \(s(t)\) tells where the object is at time \(t\); velocity tells how fast that position is changing.

Suppose a particle moves in a straight line and its position at time \(t\) is given by the function \(s(t)\). The average velocity over the interval from \(t\) to \(t_{1}\), denoted by \(v_{\text{avg}}\), is defined as:

blocks.text_alt: v average equals s of t 1 minus s of t, over t 1 minus t; equation (i)

blocks.text: Equation (i) also represents the slope of scent line passing through the points \((t, s(t))\) and \((t_{1}, s(t_{1}))\). If the interval \(t_{1} - t\) is not small, this average velocity does not accurately represent the rate of change at time \(t\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints "scent line". The correct word is "secant line": the line through the two points \((t, s(t))\) and \((t_{1}, s(t_{1}))\) of the position graph.

To illustrate this, consider a particle whose position at time \(t\) (in seconds) is given by the function \(s(t) = t^{2} + t\) in metres. The average rate of change over various time intervals starting at \(t = 3\) seconds is shown in the table below:

blocks.caption: Average velocity of the particle with s(t) = t² + t over three intervals starting at t = 3 (the book prints this table across the page with the three graphs under it)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Where do the numbers come from?
\(s(3) = 3^{2} + 3 = 12\), \(s(4) = 16 + 4 = 20\), \(s(5) = 25 + 5 = 30\)
\(s(3.5) = 12.25 + 3.5 = 15.75 = \frac{63}{4}\)
Each average velocity is the slope of a secant on the position graph: rise (change in position) ÷ run (change in time). The three graphs below show these secants as right triangles.

blocks.alt: Graph of s(t) = t squared plus t for t from 0 to about 6.7, with t marked 1 to 6 and s from 10 to 50. A red right triangle starts at the point (3, 12): its horizontal side goes to t = 5 (5 − 3 = 2) and its vertical side rises to the point (5, 30) on the curve (30 − 12 = 18). A dashed green secant joins (3, 12) and (5, 30).
blocks.caption: Graph 1 of 3: s(t) = t² + t from t = 3 to t = 5, slope of the secant = 18 ÷ 2 (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.alt: Graph of s(t) = t squared plus t for t from 0 to about 6.7, with t marked 1 to 6 and s from 10 to 50. A red right triangle starts at the point (3, 12): its horizontal side goes to t = 4 (4 − 3 = 1) and its vertical side rises to the point (4, 20) on the curve (20 − 12 = 8). A dashed green secant joins (3, 12) and (4, 20).
blocks.caption: Graph 2 of 3: s(t) = t² + t from t = 3 to t = 4, slope of the secant = 8 ÷ 1 (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.alt: Graph of s(t) = t squared plus t for t from 0 to about 6.7, with t marked 1 to 6 and s from 10 to 50. A red right triangle starts at the point (3, 12): its horizontal side goes to t = 3.5 (3.5 − 3 = 0.5) and its vertical side rises to the point (3.5, 15.75) on the curve (15.75 − 12 = 3.75). A dashed green secant joins (3, 12) and (3.5, 15.75).
blocks.caption: Graph 3 of 3: s(t) = t² + t from t = 3 to t = 3.5, slope of the secant = 3.75 ÷ 0.5 (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.text: We observe that these values do not closely approximate the particle's velocity at exactly 3 seconds. To obtain a better approximation of velocity at \(x = 3\), we use smaller intervals:

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints "velocity at \(x = 3\)". The variable here is time \(t\), so it should read "velocity at \(t = 3\)".

blocks.caption: Average velocity over smaller intervals starting at t = 3

blocks.text:
We see that as the length of the time interval decreases, the average velocity approaches the instantaneous velocity at \(t = 3\). Based on the trend, we estimate the instantaneous velocity to be approximately 7 m/sec.
Thus, over a sufficiently small interval, the velocity changes negligibly. If \(t_{1}\) is very close to \(t\), the average velocity over \(t_{1} - t\) approximates the instantaneous velocity at \(t\). As \(t_{1}\) approaches \(t\), the average velocity becomes the instantaneous velocity.
This is similar to approximating the slope of a tangent line by calculating the slope of a secant line. Mathematically, the instantaneous velocity, denoted by \(v_{\text{inst}}\), is given by the following limit:
\[v_{\text{inst}} = \lim_{t_{1} \to t} \dfrac{s(t_{1}) - s(t)}{t_{1} - t}\]
(Provide the limit exist)
For convenient, if \(t_{1} = t + \delta t\), then as \(t_{1} \to t \Rightarrow \delta t \to 0\), thus the above equation becomes:

blocks.text_alt: v instantaneous equals the limit, as delta t tends to 0, of s of t plus delta t minus s of t, over delta t; equation (ii)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Two wording slips in the print: "(Provide the limit exist)" should be "(provided the limit exists)", and "For convenient" should be "For convenience".
In other words, the instantaneous velocity is the derivative of the position function \(s(t)\) with respect to time.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The table only lets us guess "about 7". The limit (ii) gives it exactly:
\[s(3+\delta t) - s(3) = (3+\delta t)^{2} + (3+\delta t) - 12\]
\[= 7\delta t + \delta t^{2}\]
\[\dfrac{7\delta t + \delta t^{2}}{\delta t} = 7 + \delta t \to 7\]
So the instantaneous velocity at \(t = 3\) is exactly \(7\) m/sec. This also explains the table: the average velocity from \(3\) to \(3 + \delta t\) is exactly \(7 + \delta t\) (for example \(7.01\) when \(\delta t = 0.01\)).

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.problem:
A particle moves along a line such that its position after \(t\) hours is given by \(s(t) = 4t^{2} + 2t + 1\) (in miles).
(a) Find the average velocity over the interval \([2, 5]\).
(b) Find the instantaneous velocity at \(t = 3\).
steps:
Given: position \(s(t) = 4t^{2} + 2t + 1\) miles after \(t\) hours.
To find: (a) the average velocity for \(2 \le t \le 5\); (b) the instantaneous velocity at \(t = 3\).
Method: (a) is an average over an interval, so we use formula (i), \(v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{s(t_{1}) - s(t)}{t_{1} - t}\), with \(t = 2\), \(t_{1} = 5\). (b) is a velocity at one instant, so we use the limit (ii) with \(t = 3\).

Step 1: (a) Position at the two ends of the interval
\[s(5) = 4(5)^{2} + 2(5) + 1\]
\[= 100 + 10 + 1 = 111\]
\[s(2) = 4(2)^{2} + 2(2) + 1\]
\[= 16 + 4 + 1 = 21\]
Why: formula (i) needs the position at the start (\(t = 2\)) and at the end (\(t = 5\)) of the interval.

Step 2: (a) Average velocity
\[v_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{s(5) - s(2)}{5 - 2}\]
\[= \dfrac{111 - 21}{3} = \dfrac{90}{3}\]
\[= 30 \text{ miles/hour}\]
Why: average velocity = change in position ÷ time taken. Position is in miles and time in hours, so the unit is miles/hour.

Step 3: (b) Write the limit (ii) at t = 3
\[v_{\text{inst}} = \lim_{\delta t \to 0} \dfrac{s(3+\delta t) - s(3)}{\delta t}\]
Why: the instantaneous velocity is the limit of average velocities over the shrinking interval from \(3\) to \(3 + \delta t\).

Step 4: (b) Find s(3 + δt)
\[s(3+\delta t) = 4(3+\delta t)^{2} + 2(3+\delta t) + 1\]
\[= 4(9 + 6\delta t + \delta t^{2}) + 6 + 2\delta t + 1\]
\[= 36 + 24\delta t + 4\delta t^{2} + 6 + 2\delta t + 1\]
\[= 43 + 26\delta t + 4\delta t^{2}\]
Why: replace \(t\) by \(3 + \delta t\) everywhere, use \((3 + \delta t)^{2} = 9 + 6\delta t + \delta t^{2}\), then collect like terms.

Step 5: (b) Find s(3) and subtract
\[s(3) = 4(9) + 6 + 1 = 43\]
\[s(3+\delta t) - s(3) = 26\delta t + 4\delta t^{2}\]
Why: the constant \(43\) cancels, as it always must, because at \(\delta t = 0\) the difference is zero.

Step 6: (b) Cancel δt and take the limit
\[\dfrac{26\delta t + 4\delta t^{2}}{\delta t} = \dfrac{\delta t(26 + 4\delta t)}{\delta t}\]
\[= 26 + 4\delta t\]
\[v_{\text{inst}} = \lim_{\delta t \to 0}(26 + 4\delta t) = 26\]
Why: \(\delta t \ne 0\) while it approaches \(0\), so we may cancel it; after that we can put \(\delta t = 0\).

Check:
Average velocities over shrinking intervals from \(t = 3\):
\[\dfrac{s(3.1) - s(3)}{0.1} = \dfrac{45.64 - 43}{0.1} = 26.4\]
\[\dfrac{s(3.01) - s(3)}{0.01} = \dfrac{43.2604 - 43}{0.01} = 26.04\]
They approach \(26\), as found. (a) is also reasonable: \(30\) lies between the velocities at the two ends, which are \(18\) at \(t = 2\) and \(42\) at \(t = 5\) (found the same way as in (b)).
blocks.answer: (a) Average velocity over \([2, 5]\) = 30 miles/hour. (b) Instantaneous velocity at \(t = 3\) = 26 miles/hour.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Small slips in the book's printed solution: "give position function" should be "given position function", and the unit "30 miles/hours" should be "30 miles/hour".

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Average velocity over \([t, t_{1}]\): \(v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{s(t_{1}) - s(t)}{t_{1} - t}\) ...(i), the slope of a secant on the position graph.
2. Instantaneous velocity: \(v_{\text{inst}} = \lim_{\delta t \to 0} \frac{s(t+\delta t) - s(t)}{\delta t}\) ...(ii), the slope of the tangent.
3. The instantaneous velocity is the derivative of the position function with respect to time.
4. Smaller intervals give average velocities closer and closer to the instantaneous velocity.
5. Units: (unit of position) per (unit of time), e.g. m/sec, miles/hour.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Finding the average velocity as \(\frac{s(5)}{5}\) or \(\frac{s(5) + s(2)}{2}\). It is change in position ÷ change in time: \(\frac{s(5) - s(2)}{5 - 2}\).
2. Expanding \(4(3 + \delta t)^{2}\) as \((12 + 4\delta t)^{2}\). Square first, then multiply by \(4\).
3. Putting \(\delta t = 0\) before cancelling, which gives \(\frac{0}{0}\).
4. Leaving out the unit of velocity in the final answer.
